cells.tense: You are standing inside what careful tending has already produced, and you can see its shape.
cells.ask: Name one real cost of this abundance to one person today, plainly.
cells.core:
You can see how the parts of this fit together — the effort, the timing, the people who showed up, all of it. That kind of seeing doesn't come from standing outside. It comes from having worked the thing long enough that it holds a shape now, and you're inside that shape while you see it.

What's free to feed next isn't the next project. It's the next question. You've proved a method; what's open is what you're testing with it. Answer that once, honestly, and you learn more than a season of checking. What you built is real. Growing it is the part you keep, long after the abundance has been spent.
cells.sheetLine: You see the whole garden because you grew it.
cells.verb: Tending what grew until the abundance shows its fruit.
cells.place: The vantage that sees the whole pattern at once.

cells.tense: You are braced against a lean season that has not arrived and may not.
cells.ask: Choose one thing to finish before starting anything else, and finish it today.
cells.core:
There's more growing than you can point to, and you're bracing for what it will demand next. The abundance got real, so now you're ahead of it — planning the next yield, guarding against a shortfall that isn't on the calendar. Your attention arrives before the thing does, and it keeps arriving early.

The thing that matters most in the next stretch is usually right in front of you, and bracing skips past it to the thing after. You can see that it's all connected, and it is — but connection isn't urgency. Pick one thing and finish it before you start another. Let the rest stay possible. Then watch how much of the pressure was the crop's at all.
cells.sheetLine: You're harvesting a season you haven't grown yet.
cells.verb: Tending what grew until the abundance shows its fruit.

cells.tense: The growing is behind you and you are still standing at the gate.
cells.ask: Return to one thing that grew under your care and stay with it ten minutes.
cells.core:
You put things in the ground, and you may not have stayed to see what came up. There's plenty alive around you — taken care of, kept going, showing for it — and you're not in the room where it grows. Catching a whole pattern at once takes time in the same place, and you've been somewhere else, or waiting for a season that already came.

The pattern doesn't hold if you don't stand inside it long enough to receive it. Go back to one thing that grew under your care and sit with it. Not to fix it — to watch. Eventually you can tell the story of how it happened, in order. More energy isn't the missing piece. Look at something you actually grew and let it count.

cells.tense: You are already seeing how the parts connect, and you call it something else.
cells.ask: Say once, in your own words, that the thread between these results was yours to tend.
cells.core:
You're the one who noticed the connection between the parts — the timing, the missing piece, the way the pieces fit. You've done it so fluently it stopped registering as something you do. It sounds like describing the work, not like anything of yours at all.

Tracing a thread runs whether you claim it or not. What doesn't run is everything that follows from owning it: the right to be asked, the next thing you'd say yes to. That's the gap — not the tracing, the owning. Say once, plainly, that the thread between these results was yours to tend. Not loudly. Once is enough. It's the truth catching up with what's already happening.

attempts.check: The one claim the record doesn't make is that the person is enjoying the flourish itself; it only says they have one to enjoy, so the reading names the tending and the abundance without their stance toward it. A reader could reasonably say the recognition isn't theirs at all, that the pattern-caught is only workload — but the record says authorship is misattributed, so that very refusal is the scene, not a refutation of it. The asks survive a wrong read: pouring effort at one horizon, sitting long enough to track a pattern, naming one thread, and taking the abundance back from the work each land on recognisable ground regardless of whose reading of the day is right. The line that serves the writer more than the person is any sentence where the whole pattern is already known to them and merely needs saying — cut.
